report:
## Conclusion: Supported, but with caveats

The claim that consuming more olive oil reduces stroke risk is **supported by a substantial body of evidence, though causality is not definitively proven**.

**Key evidence:**

- **PREDIMED trial (Spain):** The largest randomized controlled trial of the Mediterranean diet (~7,400 high-risk participants) found that a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil reduced major cardiovascular events by roughly 30%, with stroke being the outcome most clearly reduced. The trial was partially retracted and reanalyzed in 2018 due to randomization errors, but results held. (https://www.bmj.com/content/364/bmj.l341?int_source=trendmd&int_medium=cpc&int_campaign=usage-042019)

- **Three-City Study (France):** Among 7,625 older adults followed ~5 years, intensive olive oil use was associated with a 41% lower stroke risk versus no use, corroborated by plasma oleic acid levels. (https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0b013e318220abeb)

- **Meta-analyses:** Pooled analyses of case-control, cohort, and intervention studies (>100,000 participants) found higher olive oil intake inversely associated with stroke risk. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9623257/)

- **Counterpoint:** A large U.S. cohort analysis (JACC, 2020) found olive oil lowered coronary heart disease risk but showed **no significant effect on stroke specifically**, suggesting benefits may depend on population and what fat olive oil replaces. (https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2020.02.036)

**Bottom line:** Olive oil—especially extra-virgin, as part of a Mediterranean-style diet and replacing butter/margarine—is associated with reduced stroke risk. Evidence is strong but largely observational; the one major RCT tested the overall diet, not olive oil alone.
